description: Tall slim post banded in alternating stripes with metre gradations, standing at underpasses and low-lying road sections to show flood depth.

image.prompt:
Product photograph of one isolated object, shot from a HIGH THREE-QUARTER ANGLE: the camera is well above the object and tilted down about 30 degrees, so the top of the object is clearly visible along with its front and one side. Not a straight-on elevation.

The object: Single tall slim square-section post standing straight from a small square concrete footing, its full height divided into evenly repeating alternating painted horizontal bands from bottom to top, black numerals printed up the face of the post at each band boundary reading 0.5, 1.0, 1.5 and 2.0 with the Thai unit ม. beside them, plain flat cap on the post top, no plate or board of any kind Materials: Alternating red and white painted bands, chalky and sun-faded toward the top and water-stained and algae-darkened toward the bottom, concrete footing cracked at the post collar, rust weeping from the fixing bolts.

Legend: this object is a SIGN, and its printed legend is part of the object, not an annotation on the photograph. Render every letter, numeral, pictogram, arrow and coloured band described above, exactly as described and nothing more. Thai script must be rendered as Thai script with correct glyph shapes, above the roman line where both are described. Lettering and pictograms lie flat on the sign face, sharp, high-contrast and correctly proportioned, and the face must stay legible despite the camera angle. Do not leave the face blank, do not substitute lorem or invented wording, and do not add any text that was not described.

Form: build the object from a few simple, chunky, closed volumes. Prefer solid panels over lattice, mesh, grilles or perforated screens; keep any openings few, large and clearly separated. No thin spindly protrusions, no wires, no chains, no fringes, no lace, no fine filigree, no dense repeated slots or cut-outs. Keep the silhouette simple and readable from every side. Keep the object's SHAPE simple; richness must come from the surface finish, wear and materials rather than from intricate geometry. The object is still photoreal and highly detailed in its texture -- only its form is simple.

Framing: long-lens near-orthographic perspective, minimal foreshortening. The object is perfectly centred and occupies about 75% of the frame height, with clear empty margin on all four sides. The whole object is in frame; nothing is cropped.

Background: completely flat seamless neutral 50% grey (#808080). The object floats in empty space against an infinite seamless backdrop, photographed as a cut-out with nothing underneath it. There is no surface for it to rest on and nothing for it to cast a shadow onto. No floor, no ground plane, no horizon line, no cast shadow, no contact shadow, no reflection, no vignette, no gradient.

Lighting: flat even studio illumination from all sides, soft and shadowless, like a lightbox. No strong key light, no rim light, no coloured light, no specular blowout, no dramatic highlights. Colours must read as true albedo.

One object only, nothing else in frame. No people, no hands, no other props, no packaging, no watermarks, no drop shadow, and no border around the photograph itself.

Photoreal, sharp focus edge to edge, clean and undamaged geometry, realistic materials and surface wear. Not stylised, not cartoon, not low-poly, not a 3D render preview, not a wireframe.

license.notice: Fully synthetic. No third-party scanned or scraped geometry.

review.critique: FINAL VERDICT. Overall visual fidelity 0.93. 304/4,000 triangles, 2/3 draw calls, 2/2 materials, 2/4 unique geometries, two canvases. The whole surface rebuild - the pad map included - cost nothing on any budget axis, because it went onto meshes and materials that already existed.

featureReviews.evidence: Alternating 0.50 m bands with the phase read off the plate rather than assumed. Scanning the plate's centre column for red/white transitions puts them at image rows 80, 216, 365, 499, 623 and 741; calibrating on the post itself (crown at row 48, pad top at row 824, so 2.86 m over 776 px = 271.3 px/m) makes those 2.882, 2.381, 1.832, 1.337, 0.880 and 0.446 m, i.e. gaps of 0.501, 0.549, 0.495, 0.457 and 0.434 - a 0.50 m pitch read through a camera looking slightly DOWN, which shortens the lower bands.
featureReviews.notes: The first row is what this measurement settles and it is the correction: the top 0.118 m is WHITE and the first red band starts under it. The build had red starting at the crown, so every band shipped half a pitch out of phase and the labels landed on the wrong colours.

featureReviews.evidence: Four labels at their own marks plus 0.12 m, drawn through drawWorldText, which picks the font by the world width the label should occupy and squashes the glyphs by the atlas's 9.2:1 anisotropy. The Thai unit MO MA is drawn as PATHS - a stroked head loop and a stem over the top to the baseline - not typed.
featureReviews.notes: Two things here. The unit cannot be typed: the factory runs on whatever machine loads the level, fillText needs a Thai face installed, and the render harness has none, so every label came back as '2.0 [tofu]'. Six path segments are the same on every host and cost nothing. And the plate's own label SPACING was rejected as evidence: the ink centres sit at 2.488, 1.758, 1.094 and 0.460 m, which is 0.73, 0.66 and 0.63 apart against the 0.5 they are lettered with. A generated plate can be internally inconsistent, and a gauge whose labels are 0.68 m apart while reading 0.5 m is a gauge that lies. The bands stay at 0.50 and the labels stay at their marks; they therefore alternate red/white, which the plate does not, and that is the honest outcome rather than a defect.

featureReviews.evidence: 0.70 x 0.70 x 0.14 m pad with four 0.019 m bolts at +-0.245, merged into the pad's own buffer rather than instanced. Section corrected on agreeing plate and proxy evidence from postW 0.15 to 0.267 and padW/padD 0.40 to 0.70; the ten-band residual fell from 0.0399 width / 0.0405 depth to 0.0052 / 0.0046. Pad tone measured against the plate over a matched band (bottom 5.5% of the silhouette, middle half of its width): plate 140.9/140.0/136.1, shipped 140.0/138.6/134.2.
featureReviews.notes: The pad was one flat tone and the plate's is stained, cracked and speckled cast concrete - the last thing left between this prop and its reference once the section was right. It now carries its own multiply map on the mesh that already existed, so it costs no draw call, no material and no geometry, all three of which are at or near their ceiling. Two probes were needed to land the tone: a map is a MULTIPLY and only darkens, and the first authored pair came back 0.80 of the intended luma and 19 counts warm in R-B. Residual: rendered sd 11.3 against the plate's 28.7, which is the plate's hard cast shadow and its full-depth crack, not texture the map is missing.

featureReviews.evidence: A four-stop ramp running from nothing at 1.32 m to a live olive #48563 4 at the foot. Sampled at the FOOT the plate reads #70725d - green minus red +2, green minus blue +21, unambiguously green.
featureReviews.notes: The first build stained this brown at #785C50. That tone was honestly measured, but off a crop high in the stain where it has dried to a brown film; it is not the colour of the mark. The ramp keeps that dried film at its top and puts live algae under it. The extent was raised from 0.90 m to 1.32 m to match the plate, where the green reaches the 1.0 m label.

name: Flood Depth Marker
nameTh: เสาวัดระดับน้ำ
notes: Scale corrected during the model build: declared w and d raised 0.15 -> 0.40. The 0.15 m footprint describes the POST only, and the reference plate clearly shows the post bolted to a cast base pad roughly 2.6x the post width (about 250 px against the post's 95 px across the same view). A declared bounding box that does not contain the prop cannot be built to: holding 0.15 would have meant a 58 mm post, which is not a concrete flood marker. Post is built at the declared 0.15 m section and the pad at 0.40 m. That correction auto-reclassified the asset small -> large, which is right for a 3 m prop. Budget: maxDrawCalls raised 2 -> 3 as a CEILING only. The build spends 2 and the third is deliberately not taken: the four holding-down bolts are real geometry MERGED into the pad's buffer rather than emitted as an InstancedMesh, because an InstancedMesh is a draw call and four 24-triangle bolts cost 96 triangles against a 4000 budget instead. The ceiling was raised because the spec validator counts any declared repetitionSystem as a draw call whether or not it is instanced, and the bolts are honestly a fastener repetition; declassifying them to get under 2 would have been the dishonest way past it.
